title: Section I. Of the different Species of Philosophy
author: David Hume
summary: Moral philosophy can be easy and obvious, painting virtue to move us to act, or accurate and abstruse, seeking the principles of human nature. Hume defends the second: it lends exactness to the first and to every art, and only a careful study of the understanding can drive out the false metaphysics that shelters superstition.

notes.note: In Hume's usage, the study of human nature in general (the mind, the passions, morals and society), not ethics alone. *Moral* is opposed to *natural* philosophy, the study of the physical world.

notes.on: Till a philosopher, at last, arose
notes.note: Isaac Newton (1642–1727), whose *Principia* (1687) derived the motions of the planets from the law of gravitation.
Hume's name for a map of the mind's faculties and operations, as distinct from an account of their causes.
Jean de La Bruyère (1645–1696), author of *Les Caractères* (1688), sketches of manners and character.
Nicolas Malebranche (1638–1715), the French Cartesian philosopher, author of *De la recherche de la vérité* (1674–75).
Joseph Addison (1672–1719), the essayist of *The Spectator*: Hume's example of the 'easy' philosopher, as Locke is of the abstruse one.

notes.on: when Locke shall be entirely forgotten
notes.note: John Locke (1632–1704), author of *An Essay concerning Human Understanding* (1690).
